## Digital Marketing Agency in Pune: What Google's AI Max Migration Means for Your Search Campaigns in 2026

Google began automatically migrating advertisers' campaign-level Broad Match and legacy Automatically Created Assets setups to AI Max starting 1 September 2026, and if your digital marketing agency in Pune hasn't already told you this is happening to your account, that's worth raising directly this month rather than waiting to notice a change in results. This isn't a minor interface update. It's Google closing off the old way of running broad-match Search campaigns and replacing it with a more automated system that changes how keywords, assets, and landing pages get matched to a search query — and it's happening whether or not your agency has actively opted into it.

For a Pune business paying someone else to manage Google Ads, the practical question isn't whether to resist this change — Google isn't offering that choice for campaigns already on legacy Broad Match — but whether your agency understands what AI Max actually does differently, has reviewed how it affects your specific account, and can explain the shift to you in plain terms rather than a vague "Google's updating things behind the scenes."

## What Actually Changed

**New campaign-level Broad Match and legacy Automatically Created Assets setups stopped being creatable from 3 August 2026**, across the Google Ads interface, Editor, and API alike. From that date forward, nobody — not your agency, not you directly — could set up a new campaign using the old broad-match structure. It simply isn't an option any more for new campaigns.

**Automatic migration of existing campaigns began 1 September 2026** and is rolling out gradually across the month rather than all at once. If your account has campaigns still running on the legacy setup, Google is moving them to AI Max on its own schedule, not on a date your agency necessarily controls or gets to choose.

**Dynamic Search Ads are being nudged toward the same shift**, with in-account notices starting in September 2026 encouraging advertisers to voluntarily move DSA campaigns to AI Max ahead of a fully automatic migration scheduled for February 2027, after which creating new DSA ad groups the old way goes away entirely.

**A new seven-day limit now applies to offline conversion uploads.** Conversions uploaded more than seven days after they actually occurred will still show up in your standard reporting, but Google's automated bidding systems — specifically data-driven attribution — will ignore them when calculating how to optimise your campaigns. This matters directly for any Pune business with a sales cycle involving a follow-up call, a site visit, or an offline close that takes longer than a week to confirm and report back into Google Ads, because a conversion reported outside that window now effectively doesn't exist as far as automated bidding is concerned, even though you can still see it in your dashboard.

**Standard Display campaigns are being folded into Demand Gen.** Google has signalled that Display as a distinct, separately manageable campaign type is being phased out later in 2026, with Display-style ads continuing to run, but inside Demand Gen campaigns rather than as their own product. For an agency that's built reporting and optimisation habits around Display as a discrete line item, this is a structural change to how that spend gets categorised and explained to a client, not just a rename.

## What AI Max Actually Does Differently From Old-Style Broad Match

The core shift is in how much control sits with the advertiser (or agency) versus with Google's automated systems. Old-style Broad Match Search campaigns still let an agency set specific keywords, even if Google had latitude to match them loosely against related search queries. AI Max campaigns lean further into automation — matching ads to a wider and more dynamically determined range of search intent, generating and testing more asset combinations automatically, and relying more heavily on machine-learning signals about what's likely to convert rather than a fixed keyword list an agency has hand-built and refined over time.

This isn't inherently worse than the old approach — for many advertisers, giving Google's systems more room to match intent and test assets has produced solid results, which is exactly why Google has pushed this direction across its ad products for several years now. But it does mean the specific skill an agency needs shifts: less time spent manually building exhaustive keyword lists, more time spent writing strong ad assets, structuring good landing pages, setting sensible conversion goals, and reviewing what the automated system is actually doing with the latitude it's been given.

## A Worked Illustration

Consider a Pune business that's run the same broad-match Search campaign structure for two years, built around a carefully curated list of forty keywords its agency assembled and refined over that time. Once that campaign migrates to AI Max, the underlying keyword list becomes less central to how the campaign actually serves ads — AI Max leans more on the landing page content, the ad assets provided, and Google's own signal-matching to decide what search queries to serve against, rather than treating the keyword list as the primary lever it once was.

An agency that simply lets the migration happen and continues reporting the same weekly numbers without reviewing what's changed is missing the point of the update. An agency doing this well reviews the account after migration, checks which search terms are actually triggering ads now compared to before, confirms the conversion goals set in the account genuinely reflect what the business considers valuable (a genuine sale versus, say, a low-intent newsletter signup counted the same way), and adjusts ad assets and landing pages to work with the new system rather than assuming the old keyword-centric playbook still applies unchanged.

## Why the Seven-Day Conversion Window Matters More Than It Sounds

This is the change most likely to go unnoticed until it's already affected your results, because nothing about your Google Ads dashboard visibly breaks — the conversions still appear in reports. What changes is quieter: Google's automated bidding stops learning from any conversion reported more than seven days after it happened.

For a Pune business selling a low-consideration product with an immediate online purchase, this rarely matters, because the conversion is usually reported within minutes. It matters considerably more for a business with a longer sales cycle — a service business where a lead comes in through a form, gets called back over the following days, and only converts into a confirmed sale a week or two later once reported back manually into Google Ads as an offline conversion. If that reporting lag regularly exceeds seven days, an increasing share of your genuine conversions are becoming invisible to the very systems responsible for finding you more of the same kind of customer, even though you can still see them sitting in a report.

The fix isn't complicated once you know to look for it: tighten the internal process for reporting offline conversions back into Google Ads so it happens within the seven-day window as a matter of routine, rather than in a monthly batch upload that's structurally too slow for this new rule.

## What the Display-to-Demand-Gen Shift Means for Your Reporting Specifically

For years, a standard Google Ads report has treated Display as its own line item — a specific budget allocation with its own click-through rate, cost per click, and conversion numbers a business could track over time. Once Display's inventory runs inside Demand Gen campaigns instead of as a standalone campaign type, that clean separation gets harder to maintain, because Demand Gen also serves ads across YouTube, Gmail, and Discover within the same campaign structure.

This isn't necessarily bad for performance — Demand Gen's more unified approach can let Google's systems shift budget toward whichever placement is actually converting, similar to the logic behind Performance Max. But it does mean a business used to seeing "Display: ₹15,000 spent, these results" as a distinct number needs to ask their agency directly how that visibility gets preserved once the campaign type changes. A competent agency should be able to show placement-level or channel-level detail within Demand Gen reporting, not simply fold Display's historical line item into a bigger number and describe the loss of granularity as unavoidable.

## A Practical Checklist for Reviewing Your Account After Migration

1. **Confirm which campaigns have already migrated to AI Max** and which are still pending, so you know the current state of your account rather than assuming it's uniform.
2. **Review the conversion goals set in the account** and confirm they reflect genuinely valuable actions for your business, not a mix of high- and low-intent actions treated identically.
3. **Check offline conversion upload timing** against the new seven-day attribution window if your sales cycle involves any delay between the ad click and a confirmed sale.
4. **Ask for a before-and-after comparison** of key metrics around the migration date, so any shift in performance can be attributed to the platform change rather than left unexplained.
5. **Review ad asset quality specifically** — headlines, descriptions, images — since AI Max leans more heavily on strong assets to determine what to serve than the old keyword-first approach did.
6. **Ask how Display spend will be reported once it moves into Demand Gen**, and confirm you'll still have visibility into that part of your budget specifically.

## Questions to Ask Your Digital Marketing Agency in Pune This Quarter

- **"Have any of our campaigns already been migrated to AI Max, and did you review the account after the migration happened?"** If they weren't tracking this at all, that's a meaningful gap given the September 2026 rollout timeline.
- **"How quickly are we reporting offline conversions back into the platform, and is it consistently under seven days?"** This is the kind of operational detail that's easy to overlook and directly affects bidding performance without ever showing up as an obvious red flag in a monthly report.
- **"What's our plan for Dynamic Search Ads before the February 2027 automatic migration?"** Moving voluntarily on your own timeline, with proper testing, is generally preferable to being moved automatically on Google's.
- **"Once Display campaigns move into Demand Gen, how will our reporting reflect that, so we can still see what's actually happening to that part of our spend?"** An agency should have a plan for keeping this legible in your reports, not let a platform restructuring quietly blur a line item you're used to reviewing separately.

## What This Doesn't Mean

It doesn't mean your agency has lost control of your account, and it doesn't mean manual strategy work has become pointless. AI Max shifts where the valuable manual work happens — toward asset quality, landing page relevance, accurate conversion tracking, and genuinely useful account structure — rather than eliminating the need for a skilled person managing the account altogether. An agency that treats this as "Google handles everything now, so there's less for us to actively do" is either misunderstanding the update or using it as an excuse to reduce the actual work going into your account while charging the same management fee.

It also doesn't mean every account needs to panic and rebuild from scratch. For many advertisers, the migration will run in the background with limited visible disruption, provided someone reviews the account afterward and confirms the fundamentals — conversion tracking accuracy, asset quality, landing page relevance — are solid enough for the more automated system to work with well.

### Do I need to approve this migration, or is it happening automatically regardless?

For campaigns already using the legacy campaign-level Broad Match or Automatically Created Assets setup, the migration to AI Max is automatic and rolling out through September 2026 without requiring separate approval from the advertiser. The decision point that's still yours is what happens after migration — whether your agency reviews and adjusts the account to work well under the new system, or leaves it running unreviewed.

### Will this change increase or decrease what I'm paying for ad spend?

There's no fixed answer, because it depends on your specific industry, competition, and how well your account is set up for the more automated approach — this is exactly the kind of question a competent agency should be able to speak to for your account specifically rather than in generalities, after reviewing your actual post-migration performance.

### Should I ask my agency to move away from Google Ads because of these changes?

Not on this basis alone. These changes reflect where Google's Search advertising product is heading generally, not a reason specific to your account to abandon the channel — most competitors in your space are working through the same shift, and Search intent traffic remains valuable regardless of how it's packaged into campaign types.

### We paused our Google Ads campaigns months ago — does any of this still apply when we restart them?

Yes. If a paused campaign was built on the legacy campaign-level Broad Match or Automatically Created Assets structure, it's still subject to the same migration rules once reactivated, and depending on timing it may already have been migrated to AI Max while sitting paused. It's worth having your agency check the campaign's current setup before simply switching it back on, rather than assuming it will behave exactly as it did when you paused it.

### What if my agency says this doesn't affect us because we don't use Broad Match?

That's possible and worth confirming rather than dismissing, but it's also worth checking directly rather than accepting it without verification — ask specifically which match types and campaign structures are active in your account today, since match-type strategy is exactly the kind of detail that can shift over a long agency relationship without a client necessarily being told about it each time.

## Where This Fits Into Your Broader Digital Marketing Plan

This connects to a wider set of platform shifts worth tracking with any digital marketing agency in Pune you're evaluating or already working with. Our broader guide on [choosing a digital marketing agency in Pune](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-guide-2026) covers how to evaluate reporting practices and channel selection more generally, and our piece on [Performance Max's channel-level reporting changes](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-performance-max-2026) covers a related transparency shift within Google's automated campaign types that's worth understanding alongside this one.

## How We Approach This at Govindani Infotech

Our [Google Ads](/services/google-ads) team reviews every account after a platform-level change like this one, rather than assuming a migration Google runs automatically needs no follow-up attention from us. When campaigns move to AI Max, we check conversion goal accuracy, asset quality, and landing page relevance specifically, because those are the levers that actually matter once the system leans more heavily on automated matching. We also audit offline conversion reporting timelines with clients who have longer sales cycles, specifically to catch the seven-day attribution window problem before it quietly erodes campaign performance.

If you want a second opinion on how the AI Max migration has affected your account, or whether your current agency's reporting reflects what's actually changed, get in touch through our [contact page](/contact-us) and we'll walk through your account with you directly.
